claims.text: Half the nation's molding-machine setters work in this one industry (standfirst); 10.9% of the industry's jobs are molding-machine setters, one job in nine (first hero stat card).
claims.source: BLS National Employment Matrix, industry 326000, 2024 base
claims.assert: (lambda s: 8.5 <= 100 / s['pct_of_industry'] <= 9.6 and 47.5 <= s['pct_of_occupation'] <= 54.9)(one(m for m in D['mix'] if m['soc'] == '51-4072'))
claims.actual: (lambda s: (s['pct_of_industry'], s['pct_of_occupation']))(one(m for m in D['mix'] if m['soc'] == '51-4072'))
claims.falsified_if: The industry's share of the occupation leaves 47.5-54.9%, at which point 'half' becomes 'about half' or a different fraction; or the setters' share of the industry leaves the 10.4-11.8% band that rounds to one job in nine, which the stat card computes rather than states. Both move with each matrix release.

claims.text: Can the region staff, pay and replace the jobs that make it a polymer capital? The industry runs mostly on floor work, and all four Northeast Ohio metros pay the degree occupations under the national rate (standfirst).
claims.source: BLS National Employment Matrix production share; BLS OEWS May 2024 median-wage ratios by education group, four metros
claims.assert: D['mix_totals']['production_share_pct'] > 50 and len(D['pay_totals']['ratio_by_metro']) == 4 and all(v['degree_median_ratio'] < 1 for v in D['pay_totals']['ratio_by_metro'].values())
claims.actual: (D['mix_totals']['production_share_pct'], {a: v['degree_median_ratio'] for a, v in D['pay_totals']['ratio_by_metro'].items()})
claims.falsified_if: Production occupations fall to half or less of the industry ('runs mostly on floor work' fails), any of the four metros' degree-group median wage ratio reaches 1.0 ('under the national rate' fails), or the wage file stops publishing one of the four metros, at which point 'all four' is a claim about a set the page no longer shows.

claims.text: 10.9% of the industry's jobs are molding-machine setters, which the first card renders as one job in nine; 51% of the nation's MOLDING-MACHINE setters (the card label now carries the full occupation name, since the page shows six other setter occupations) work in plastics and rubber manufacturing; 725,100 jobs in the industry nationally in 2024, the base the 10.9% and 4.2% are cut from; engineers, scientists and technicians are 4.2% of jobs in the industry. All four cards carry a United States stamp: the fourth used to gloss 4.2% as 'the jobs the region claims distinction in', a regional referent hung on a national share.
claims.source: BLS National Employment Matrix, industry 326000, 2024 base
claims.assert: (lambda s: s['pct_of_industry'] == 10.9 and round(s['pct_of_occupation']) == 51 and round(100 / s['pct_of_industry']) == 9)(one(m for m in D['mix'] if m['soc'] == '51-4072')) and D['mix_totals']['industry_emp_2024_k'] == 725.1 and D['mix_totals']['eng_sci_share_pct'] == 4.2
claims.actual: (one(m for m in D['mix'] if m['soc'] == '51-4072')['pct_of_industry'], one(m for m in D['mix'] if m['soc'] == '51-4072')['pct_of_occupation'], D['mix_totals']['industry_emp_2024_k'], D['mix_totals']['eng_sci_share_pct'])
claims.falsified_if: Any of the four hero figures changes in the next matrix release, or the setters' share stops rounding to one job in nine (the card computes the denominator from the share and prints the word for it, so a share of 11.9% would print 'one job in eight' without anyone editing the page). The engineer/scientist/technician share is the sum of detailed occupations with codes 17-2, 19-2, 19-4 and 17-3; a code added to or dropped from the matrix changes it.

claims.text: The fourteen LARGEST occupations are 60% of the industry, and most of them are on the floor (staffing h2). The fourteen shown hold 432,200 of the industry's 725,100 jobs, which is 59.6%; the shares printed on the bars sum to 59.4% because each is rounded to a tenth of a point, and the table note prints both with the reason they differ. Production occupations of every kind are 58.7%.
claims.source: BLS National Employment Matrix, industry 326000, 2024 base
claims.assert: len(D['mix']) == 14 and abs(pct(sum(m['emp_2024_k'] for m in D['mix']), D['mix_totals']['industry_emp_2024_k']) - 59.6) < 0.05 and round(pct(sum(m['emp_2024_k'] for m in D['mix']), D['mix_totals']['industry_emp_2024_k'])) == 60 and abs(sum(m['pct_of_industry'] for m in D['mix']) - 59.4) < 0.005 and abs(pct(sum(m['emp_2024_k'] for m in D['mix']), D['mix_totals']['industry_emp_2024_k']) - sum(m['pct_of_industry'] for m in D['mix'])) > 0.1 and D['mix_totals']['production_share_pct'] == 58.7 and sum(1 for m in D['mix'] if m['soc'].startswith('51-')) >= 8 and len([m for m in D['mix'] if m['soc'] not in D['education_totals']['hs_majority']]) == 4
claims.actual: (len(D['mix']), pct(sum(m['emp_2024_k'] for m in D['mix']), D['mix_totals']['industry_emp_2024_k']), sum(m['pct_of_industry'] for m in D['mix']), D['mix_totals']['production_share_pct'])
claims.falsified_if: The top-fourteen share stops computing to 59.6% from the job counts, stops rounding to the 60% the h2 prints, or the bar shares stop summing to the 59.4% the note prints beside it. A reader added the fourteen job counts, divided by 725,100 and got 59.6% against a printed 59.4%, and was right: the old figure was the sum of fourteen shares each rounded down to a tenth of a point. Both numbers are now printed with the reason they differ, so this assert holds the PAIR rather than either half, and the third clause fails if they ever stop differing, at which point the note explaining the gap would be describing a gap that is not there. Also fails if fewer than eight of the fourteen are production occupations, or the two fourteen-member sets on this page stop differing by four members.

claims.text: Rows on the staffing chart and its table run largest first by JOB COUNT, not by the rounded share the bar prints, so cutting-and-press machine setters (14,600 jobs) sits above industrial engineers (14,400) even though both print 2.0%.
claims.source: BLS National Employment Matrix, industry 326000, 2024 base: employment by occupation

A reader counting down the chart found industrial engineers printed above an occupation with 200 more jobs, because the file breaks a tie on the rounded share by something the page does not show. The order is now derived from the counts.

claims.text: The largest floor job alone outweighs every engineer and scientist in the industry combined (mix figure title), drawn as a reference rule at the summed engineer, scientist and technician share of 4.2%, labelled with the five occupations that pass it on their own.
claims.source: BLS National Employment Matrix: setters' share vs the summed engineer/scientist/technician share
claims.assert: (lambda s: s['pct_of_industry'] > D['mix_totals']['eng_sci_share_pct'] and s['soc'].startswith('51-') and s['pct_of_industry'] == max(m['pct_of_industry'] for m in D['mix']))(one(m for m in D['mix'] if m['soc'] == '51-4072')) and len([m for m in D['mix'] if m['pct_of_industry'] > D['mix_totals']['eng_sci_share_pct']]) == 5

claims.text: The twelve counties reported 18,594 plastics-and-rubber jobs in 2024. Applying the national shares gives about 2,000 molding-machine setters and about 780 engineers, scientists and technicians, on a stated assumption (staffing-pattern note beside the mix chart).
claims.source: BLS QCEW 2024 annual averages, private ownership, NAICS 326, the twelve PIC-12 counties; shares from the National Employment Matrix

claims.source: BLS OEWS May 2024, metropolitan and national files, annual median
claims.assert: (lambda B: B == {'10420': 5, '17410': 11, '15940': 5, '49660': 1})({a: len([r for r in D['pay'] if not r['metros'][a]['absent'] and r['national'] and r['metros'][a]['median'] > r['national']['median']]) for a in ['10420', '17410', '15940', '49660']}) and D['pay_totals']['disclosed'] == {'10420': 25, '17410': 25, '15940': 22, '49660': 21} and len([r for r in D['pay'] for a in ['10420', '17410', '15940', '49660'] if not r['metros'][a]['absent'] and r['national'] and r['metros'][a]['median'] == r['national']['median']]) == 2 and D['pay_totals']['beats_national']['17410'] == 10 and (lambda r: r['metros']['17410']['median'] - r['national']['median'] == 30 and round(r['metros']['17410']['median_vs_us'], 2) == 1.0)(one(p for p in D['pay'] if p['soc'] == '51-1011'))
claims.actual: ({a: len([r for r in D['pay'] if not r['metros'][a]['absent'] and r['national'] and r['metros'][a]['median'] > r['national']['median']]) for a in ['10420', '17410', '15940', '49660']}, D['pay_totals']['beats_national'], D['pay_totals']['disclosed'])
claims.falsified_if: A new wage vintage moves any metro median across the national one, or changes which cells are published. The lede used to print a typed 10 for Cleveland; a reader counting the published table got 11 and was right. The stored beats_national field is computed on each row's ratio ROUNDED to two places, so first-line supervisors at $71,220 against $71,190 read as 1.00 and dropped out, while the page's own paycheck band celebrates a $30 lead in Akron as beating the nation. The page now counts in dollars and this assert reproduces that count. The two clauses about the stored field and the supervisors' cell are the tripwire: if a rebuild fixes beats_national upstream, this fails and whoever sees it can delete the divergence note rather than leave two counts on one page. Ties are excluded by design and named in the table note, so the tie count is asserted too.

claims.text: The pay gap against the nation is widest at the top of the schooling ladder (pay h2); the degree band sits deeper under its diamonds than the floor band in every metro (figure title); the on-chart band notes read Akron pays these 7% under the nation (0.93x) and Cleveland 5% under (0.95x) for the degree band, against Akron 3% under (0.97x) and Cleveland 1% over (1.01x) for the high-school band, with the middle band carrying the same summary for the first time (guarded separately by occ-mid-band-note). Each row also prints its metro-over-nation ratio in a right-hand column, because a $30 gap and a $16,200 gap are the same picture on one dollar scale.
claims.source: BLS OEWS May 2024 (metro median / national median), grouped by the O*NET education majority
claims.assert: all(v['degree_median_ratio'] < v['hs_median_ratio'] for v in D['pay_totals']['ratio_by_metro'].values()) and len(D['education_totals']['ba_plus_majority']) == 6 and len(D['education_totals']['hs_majority']) == 14 and round(D['pay_totals']['ratio_by_metro']['10420']['degree_median_ratio'], 2) == 0.93 and round(D['pay_totals']['ratio_by_metro']['10420']['hs_median_ratio'], 2) == 0.97 and round(D['pay_totals']['ratio_by_metro']['17410']['degree_median_ratio'], 2) == 0.95 and round(D['pay_totals']['ratio_by_metro']['17410']['hs_median_ratio'], 2) == 1.01 and round((1 - D['pay_totals']['ratio_by_metro']['10420']['degree_median_ratio']) * 100) == 7 and round((1 - D['pay_totals']['ratio_by_metro']['17410']['degree_median_ratio']) * 100) == 5 and round((1 - D['pay_totals']['ratio_by_metro']['10420']['hs_median_ratio']) * 100) == 3 and round((D['pay_totals']['ratio_by_metro']['17410']['hs_median_ratio'] - 1) * 100) == 1

Canton-Massillon and Youngstown-Warren rest on three degree occupations each; a single published cell changes them.

Those are two different fourteens: four of the largest occupations are not high-school-majority jobs (default selector verdict).
claims.source: BLS National Employment Matrix; BLS OEWS May 2024 ratios by education group
claims.assert: D['pay_totals']['occupations'] == 26 and D['mix_totals']['top_n'] == 14 and abs(pct(sum(m['emp_2024_k'] for m in D['mix']), D['mix_totals']['industry_emp_2024_k']) - 59.6) < 0.05 and all(v['degree_median_ratio'] < v['hs_median_ratio'] for v in D['pay_totals']['ratio_by_metro'].values()) and len([m for m in D['mix'] if m['soc'] not in D['education_totals']['hs_majority']]) == 4

The count of largest-but-not-high-school-majority occupations is printed as a word and read from the data, so it cannot go stale silently. Per the house pattern for interactive verdicts, this guards the DEFAULT sentence; per-occupation variants recompose from the same data fields and are unguarded by design.

'High-school-majority' rather than 'high-school jobs' wherever the industry's fourteen LARGEST occupations are also in view.

Its 'most-reported level' cell prints one of the survey's twelve levels and says which of the table's four columns holds it.
claims.source: O*NET 30.3 Education element 2.D.1, the twelve required-level categories, joined to the federal occupation code
claims.assert: [r['soc'] for r in D['education'] if r.get('bins') and r['join'].split(' ')[1][:7] != r['soc']] == ['51-2090'] and one(r for r in D['education'] if r['soc'] == '51-2090')['onet_title'] == 'Team Assemblers' and all(1 <= r['modal']['category'] <= 12 for r in D['education'] if r.get('bins')) and one(r for r in D['education'] if r['soc'] == '49-9071')['modal']['category'] in (3, 4, 5) and one(r for r in D['education'] if r['soc'] == '17-3026')['modal']['category'] in (3, 4, 5) and all(r['bins'][('hs_or_less' if r['modal']['category'] <= 2 else 'some_college' if r['modal']['category'] <= 5 else 'bachelors' if r['modal']['category'] <= 7 else 'graduate')] + 0.05 >= r['modal']['pct'] for r in D['education'] if r.get('bins'))

claims.falsified_if: A later O*NET release joins another federal code to a differently-numbered database occupation (the occupation column would then have a second row naming two titles, which is correct, but this assert names the one that exists today), or the modal level leaves the 1-12 numbering the four columns are cut from. That numbering is what makes the column each modal level belongs to derivable rather than guessable: levels 1-2 are high school or less, 3-5 some college or associate, 6-7 bachelor's, 8-12 graduate. Before this pass the table printed the database title 'Team Assemblers' under a heading every other surface fills with 'Assemblers and fabricators', and printed modal levels ('Post-Secondary Certificate', 'Some College Courses') that appear among none of the four column heads above them; a reader gave up reconciling the row. The two named rows are the ones that produced those labels. The last clause runs the same 1-2 / 3-5 / 6-7 / 8-12 mapping the page uses and checks that the column each cell names really does contain that level's share, so a re-binning upstream cannot leave the parenthetical pointing at the wrong column.
